stimulus.source_note: Bartolome de las Casas, A Brief Account of the Destruction of the Indies (written 1542, published 1552; this English translation, 1689). Text verbatim from Project Gutenberg EBook #20321. Archaic spelling kept.
stimulus.text: Finally, in one word, their Ambition and Avarice, than which the heart of Man never entertained greater, and the vast Wealth of those Regions; the Humility and Patience of the Inhabitants (which made their approach to these Lands more facil and easie) did much promote the business: Whom they so despicably contemned, that they treated them (I speak of things which I was an Eye Witness of, without the least fallacy) not as Beasts, which I cordially wished they would, but as the most abject dung and filth of the Earth.

stem: Historians rely on Las Casas's writings as evidence of Spanish cruelty, but they also know he wrote to persuade the Crown to reform. Which statement best reflects how historians should use his account?

options.text: It is a Spanish critic's view of the conquest, but its claims must be weighed against his reformist purpose.

options.misconception: Treats a persuasive purpose as proof the author was never there.
options.text: It is useless as historical evidence because Las Casas never actually visited the Americas himself.

options.misconception: Treats the author's job as a substitute for checking evidence.
options.text: It should be accepted uncritically because its author was a Catholic priest.

options.misconception: Turns one critic into a spokesman for every Spaniard.
options.text: It proves that every single Spaniard living anywhere in the Americas actively and openly opposed the encomienda system.

instruction: Answer from the stimulus and stem only. Pick one option. Do not open the question file.
